## Running apps at home with containers

Running containers is not only for data analysis.
Many people run apps for their own home in containers,
on an always-on computer such as an old laptop, a mini PC or a Raspberry Pi,
which is often called a *home lab*.
Each app below publishes a container image,
so trying one uses the same `docker pull`, `docker run` and `docker compose` commands as the earlier chapters.
Many of them give you a `docker-compose.yml` file to start from,
and several (Firefly III, Wardrowbe, Immich, Paperless-ngx and TeslaMate)
run as a few containers that work together,
like the services in [Docker Compose](0650-containers-docker-compose.qmd).
Each app's name links to its instructions for running it with Docker.

## Managing many containers

Once you run several apps,
a web page that shows all of your containers helps.
[Portainer](https://docs.portainer.io/start/install-ce/server/docker/linux) (`portainer/portainer-ce`)
is the best known one,
and its Community Edition is open source.
[Dockhand](https://dockhand.pro) (`fnsys/dockhand`) is a newer alternative.
Both start, stop and update containers and Compose stacks,
and show their logs, from your browser.
Dockhand is free for personal use, such as a home lab,
and for schools and universities,
but businesses pay to use it in production.

Both run with Docker's socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) mounted into their container,
which lets them control every container on the computer.
Only give that access to tools you trust.

:::{.callout-warning}
Keep home-lab apps on your home network.
Opening a port on your router to reach them from outside
puts them on the internet, where anyone can try to log in.
To reach them when you are away, use a private network (VPN) instead,
such as [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com/kb/1282/docker).
:::
